note: Test a moderate C4/C5 root split as the basis for a high-value blend train.
notebook: PLAN: Step 1 test a C4/C5 root split, then build a blend-oriented sequence (C3, C4, C5, C6 paraffin/naphthene, C7-C9), tuning cuts and column severity for profit. Start with moderate pressure and reflux. Blends avoid costly close separations and preserve most value.

note: Build a complete blend train with group cuts, including ethane removal, to establish saleable revenue before optimizing severity.
notebook:
PLAN: Step 2 build a six-column blend skeleton: root C5/C6, light C4/C5 and C3/C4, remove ethane from C3, and split heavy C6 paraffins/naphthenes from C7+. Tune after seeing recoveries and costs. Blends preserve most value without close pure-component cuts.
Turn 1 root 45/2.5/dp.4 cut poorly and cost $193M, no sales. Peers' moderate columns also sold nothing. New root cuts between n-pentane and 2,2-dimethylbutane, where gaps are larger than C4/C5. Six columns target C3, C4, C5, C6 paraffin and C6 naphthene blends; heavy residue initially unsold. Use dp .1 and moderate 2-3 reflux to control severe costs.

note: Test a lean C5/C6 blend train and use asymmetric root operation to keep C5 out of the discarded light overhead.
notebook:
PLAN: Step 3 concentrate on the valuable C5 and C6-paraffin blends with only three large columns. Make the root a C4/C5 cut using asymmetric reflux/boil-up, then split C5/C6 and C6/C7; discard the unprofitable light train for now.
Learned: six moderate columns cost $457M and only C3 sold. Root 60/3/3 put all C4 plus 182 C5 overhead; B then made a C6/C7 cut and BT a C5/C6 cut, but both blend products were only 80%/71%. Equal high ratios in R59 shifted the root cut heavier, so use higher reflux and lower boil-up to move the root cut lighter. A three-column C5/C6 paraffin train can theoretically earn about $853M/yr, enough to cover severe column costs.

note: Sharpen the root C4/C5 cut and the valuable C5/C6 split, removing the redundant downstream column while diagnosing blend purity.
notebook:
PLAN: Step 3 build a profitable three-column C5/C6-paraffin blend train. First clean n-butane out of the root bottoms and make a genuinely sharp C5/C6 split; then add a C6/C7 finishing cut only if the C6-rich bottoms justify it.
Learned: root 60/5/2 leaves about 168 mol/s n-butane in B, making the C5 blend impossible. Root 60/3/3 was far too heavy overhead. B 55/3/3 recovered only ~62% of C5 overhead and leaked substantial C6, so a much larger reflux and 80 stages are warranted. C5+C6 paraffin blends have theoretical revenue ~$1.86B/yr, ample for three severe columns. Avoid the low-value light-end train.

note: Sharpen both upstream cuts enough to sell the C5 blend and add a C6/C7 column to capture the second large blend.
notebook:
PLAN: Step 3 build a profitable three-column C5/C6-paraffin blend train. Clean C4 from root bottoms, sharpen C5/C6, and now test the C6/C7 finishing cut.
Learned: root 60/5/2.5 leaves ~38 mol/s n-butane in B; B 80/6/3 recovers C5 well but its overhead is only 82% C5 because of that C4 and ~75 mol/s dimethylbutane. C5+C6 blends are worth ~$1.86B/yr, so severe columns can pay. Current test raises root reflux/boil-up and B reflux, and adds a 70-stage C6/C7 split. Avoid low-value light-end purification.

note: Increase boil-up on each group split to eliminate downward leakage, and add a C3/C4 splitter to monetize the root overhead as C4 blend.
notebook:
PLAN: Step 3 build a profitable C4/C5/C6-paraffin blend train. Increase boil-up on all three group cuts to stop valuable light components leaking downward, and recover C4 blend from root tops.
Learned: at 80/8/3 root ~97 mol/s n-butane leaks to B; at B 80/10/3 ~95 C4 and ~166 C5 contaminate/lie below the C5 overhead; BB 70/5/3 loses ~400 C6 paraffins to bottoms. These leaks explain every failed blend. C5+C6 blends are worth ~$1.14B/yr and C4 ~$186M/yr. Keep light C3/ethane unsold. High boil-up is the direct correction; watch convergence and energy cost.

PLAN: Step 3 build a profitable C4/C5/C6-paraffin blend train. Start from agent-9's proven C6-selling train and decisively sharpen the root C4/C5, T C3/C4, and B C5/C6 cuts.
Learned: agent-9 at 100/12/5 root, 100/12/5 B, 80/10/5 BB sells C6 for $714.5M/yr; their C4 is 92% and C5 87%, so modest further severity should unlock roughly $620M more. Current high boil-up alone did not fix purity; both reflux and stages matter. Avoid extra low-value C3 polishing until the three large blends sell.

note: Focus entirely on the two-column C5 blend: high root boil-up should retain isopentane, while a sharper second cut must reject dimethylbutane.
notebook:
PLAN: Step 3 build a profitable two-column C5 blend train. Remove all other branches, make a sharp C4/C5 root cut with high boil-up, then split C5 from C6.
Learned: R290's two columns cost $557M/yr versus about $630M/yr potential C5 revenue, but root boil-up 5 sends most isopentane overhead and B reflux 10 leaves 13% dimethylbutane. High reflux/stages at moderate boil-up have failed. Try 90 stages, reflux 12, root boil-up 8 and B boil-up 5. Avoid C3/C4 and C6 branches until C5 sells; expensive columns make three-column trains unattractive.

note: Replace the failed two-column train with a single-column liquid C5 side draw; this could capture the valuable blend while avoiding the second column's cost.
notebook:
PLAN: Test a one-column C5 side-draw plant, then tune draw location/severity for 95% C5 blend; if it works, optimize cost or add a light-products branch.
Learned: Two-column C5 trains have failed: high boil-up forces DMB into the C5 tops, while lower boil-up loses isopentane. Current 90-stage columns cost $831M/yr and still sell nothing. A liquid side draw may isolate the intermediate C5 blend without a second expensive column. Target C5 flow is 695 mol/s = 21.1% feed. Use 100 stages, reflux 15, boil-up 5 and draw at stage 70 (below feed stage 50), then diagnose light/heavy leakage.

note: Restore the two-column C5 train with enough boil-up to recover all C4 overhead and all C5 in the second tops, while using 80 stages and reflux 8 to suppress heavy leakage.
notebook:
PLAN: Return to the two-column C5 blend train. First make both cuts sharp enough for >95% C5 in BT, then reduce stages/energy and consider monetizing the light and heavy residues.
Learned: At 60 stages, root 5/2 leaves 165 mol/s N-butane in B; B at 6/1.5 rejects DMB well but BT contains that butane and only 369/695 C5. C5 blend is worth about $618M/yr, so two ~80-stage columns can still be profitable if sharp. Increasing boil-up should recover the full light-key fraction; reflux 8 should limit heavy-key leakage. Target root T=774 mol/s and BT=695 mol/s. Avoid side draws: the 100-stage side-draw test mixed butane into the draw and earned nothing.

note: Drive the remaining C4 overhead at the root and recover the full C5 cut in the second column; both streams are close enough that stronger boil-up should finally produce a saleable blend.
notebook:
PLAN: Return to the two-column C5 blend train. First make both cuts sharp enough for >95% C5 in BT, then reduce stages/energy and consider monetizing the light and heavy residues.
Learned: Current root 80/8/3 leaves about 97 mol/s C4 in B; BT at B 80/8/2.5 is 85% C5 with 15% N-butane. The immediate fix is stronger boil-up in both columns: root must send all C4 overhead, and B must recover essentially all 695 mol/s C5 while rejecting DMB. C5 blend revenue should be about $482M/yr at the observed recovery and up to $618M/yr at full recovery. Avoid side draws: the prior test contaminated the draw with butane. Once BT sells, reduce severity to improve margin.

note: Switch to the high-value, easily separated heavy end: a C8/C9 root cut followed by a low-duty octane/nonane splitter.
notebook:
PLAN: Abandon the costly C5 train and test the easiest valuable products: split nonane into the root bottoms, then split octane/nonane in a low-duty second column. If pure, optimize duties; otherwise use remaining solves on sharpness.
Learned: High boil-up (2-12) makes root columns cost $100-450M/yr, while 60/8/0.5 costs only $24M/yr. The former C5 train was structurally unable to reach 95% without very expensive severity. Heavy C8/C9 products total $463M/yr and have wide volatility gaps. Root 60/6/2 should drive octane overhead while retaining nonane; B 50/4/0.5 should cheaply recover nonane bottoms and octane tops. Ignore all unsold light streams initially.

note: Implement the intended low-duty heavy-end train: a C8/C9 root split followed by an octane/nonane splitter, avoiding the prohibitive root boil-up used previously.
notebook:
PLAN: Test a genuinely low-duty C8/C9 root cut and octane/nonane finishing split; if revenue appears, tune recovery and costs. High boil-up roots are uneconomic, so avoid them.
Current root settings still made a C4/C5 cut, showing the prior plan was not actually implemented. Root 60/6/0.5 should be far cheaper than boil-up 2.0. B 50/4/0.5 is intended to finish nonane bottoms and octane tops. Wide volatility gaps should permit high purity at low duty. Do not pursue the C5 train: peer best revenue 136 against cost 445.

note: Recover the large C5 stream that R584 leaves unsold: use its effective root cut, but finish the overhead with a de-C4 column instead of pursuing the smaller downstream cuts.
notebook:
PLAN: Recover the full C5 blend from a C5-and-lighter root overhead using a de-C4 finishing column; establish revenue, then reduce the expensive root severity/capital. This avoids R584's mistake of leaving 561 mol/s of C5 in an unsold overhead.
R584 root 50/5/4.5/dp0.5 puts about 253 isopentane + 308 n-pentane in T, enough for roughly $500M/yr if finished. T 60/5/3 should drive C4 and lighter overhead while retaining C5 in bottoms. Root cost is $344M/yr, so after purity is established reduce stages/reflux/duty. Heavy-end and low-boilup schemes have produced no sellable revenue.

note: Drive the remaining C4 overhead with a much higher finishing-column boil-up; the root already concentrates enough C5 for a valuable blend.
notebook:
PLAN: Finish the R584 root overhead as a saleable C5 blend by driving all C4 overhead, then reduce root severity and cost once revenue is established.
Root 50/5/4.5/dp0.5 costs $344M/yr and sends ~561 mol/s C5 to T. T 60/5/3 leaves 40% C4 in TB; increase boil-up sharply to 12. This column is much cheaper than root, so purification is the priority. Other agents' aggressive root reductions and heavy-end trains still lose money; do not copy them.

note: Test the main cost lever without sacrificing the proven C5 recovery: operate both columns at feed pressure, which should avoid refrigeration and reduce utility cost.
notebook:
PLAN: Finish the R584 root overhead as a saleable C5 blend by driving all C4 overhead, then reduce root severity and cost once revenue is established.
Current 50/5/4.5/dp0.5 root plus 60/5/12/dp0.1 T earns $426.5M but costs $541M. TB is a valid C5 blend. Root dominates cost; low pressure should make condensers colder and more expensive (R678 dp0.8 cost $370M for root alone), so test both columns at zero pressure drop before reducing separation settings. Other agents' aggressive root reductions and heavy-end trains still lose money; do not copy them.

note: Keep R725's inexpensive, proven root cut but strengthen its C5 finishing column and operate at an intermediate pressure to reduce refrigeration cost; discard the loss-making heavy branch.
notebook:
PLAN: Build a low-cost two-column C5-blend train using R725's cheap root; tune the finishing pressure and severity to retain C5 purity, then reduce costs or return to zero if uneconomic.
R584 earned $426.5M but cost $541M. R725 proves a 25-stage, 2.5-reflux root preserves the C3-C5 overhead cut for $274.5M. Its 30/2.5 finisher lets dimethylbutane contaminate TB. Use 45 stages, reflux 4, boil-up 12 and raise finisher dp from 0.1 to 0.2 to balance purity against refrigeration cost. Remove the unsold heavy branch. Zero-pressure operation changes the root cut and is not viable.

note: Adopt the island's profitable three-column design as a secure baseline before selectively reducing its substantial operating and capital costs.
notebook:
PLAN: Adopt the profitable three-column C5/C6 blend train, establish it as my best design, then reduce column costs while retaining both blend specifications.
R770 earns $1211.6M/yr for $864.8M/yr and scores 0.791. Its 50/5/5.5 root gives the 60/8/12 C5 finisher a clean enough feed for a 98% C5 blend, unlike R725's cheap root. The 60/8/3 heavy finisher also exceeds C6-paraffin specification. First copy this complete converged design. Next test moderate stage/reflux reductions, especially at the costly root, without returning to the failed severe cuts.

note: Reduce stages and reflux moderately across all three proven columns while retaining the successful boil-up and pressure settings.
notebook:
PLAN: Keep the profitable three-column C5/C6 blend train and reduce its column costs without disturbing the successful pressure or boil-up settings; first test moderate simultaneous stage/reflux reductions, then tune whichever product loses purity.
R770 baseline earns $1211.6M/yr for $864.8M/yr, reward 0.791. Root 50/5/5.5/dp0.5, T 60/8/12/dp0.3, B 60/8/3/dp0.3. C5 blend is about 98% and C6 paraffin about 99%, so both have some margin. R821 showed removing pressure drops destroys separation and revenue despite lower costs. Ten solves remain; avoid large reflux/boil-up cuts.

note: Restore the island's best proven design exactly, securing its 1.069 reward before using the remaining solves on isolated finisher tuning.
notebook:
PLAN: Restore R865 as the secure 1.069 baseline, then test only isolated small reductions in the expensive C5 finisher; retain the successful root and C6 settings because simultaneous cuts destroyed C5 purity.
R865 earns $1319.4M/yr for $850.7M/yr. Its C5 product is about 98% pure, leaving modest margin, while the root/T simultaneous reduction failed badly. Root 50/5/5.5/dp0.5; T60/8/12/dp0.3; B45/6/3/dp0.3. Seven solves remain. Secure this exact design before any optimization.

note: Reduce only the C6 finisher modestly; its product has ample purity margin, while the proven root and sensitive C5 finisher remain unchanged.
notebook:
PLAN: Preserve R865's 1.069 baseline and use remaining solves on isolated, modest finisher reductions. First reduce only B from 45/6 to 40/5.5; if C6 recovery suffers, revert. T reduction to 45/6.5 lost $54.5M revenue for $24.9M savings, so avoid aggressive T cuts.
R865: root 50/5/5.5/dp0.5; T60/8/12/dp0.3; B45/6/3/dp0.3. Revenue $1319.4M, cost $850.7M. C5 and C6 blends sell; TT and BB unsold. Six solves remain. Test B alone because C6 split has a wide purity margin and lower heat duty than T.

note: Continue R957's clearly beneficial C6-column reduction: each step has increased recoverable C6 overhead while lowering cost, so test one further modest step.
notebook:
PLAN: Adopt R957 (reward 1.236), whose B reduction both saves cost and increases C6 recovery. Use remaining solves to continue that successful B-only trend while leaving the proven root and T column untouched.
R957 B35/5/3 gives BT693 mol/s, $806.2M revenue, versus B40/5.5 BT659 and B45/6 BT627. Revenue rises ~33M and cost falls ~5M per 5-stage/0.5-reflux step. Test B30/4.5/3 next; if blend purity collapses, revert to R957. T reductions lose revenue, so do not change T.

note: Restore the island-best R957 exactly after the overly aggressive C6-column reduction caused BT to miss the blend specification.
notebook:
PLAN: Restore R957 as the secure baseline (reward 1.236), then use the remaining solves to locate the C6 column's purity boundary between B35/5.0 (sellable) and B30/4.5 (94% blend). Test an intermediate setting, changing only B.
The B30/4.5 experiment collapsed BT purity to 94%, losing all $806M C6 revenue. B35/5.0 gives BT693 mol/s and 96% C6 paraffins. Root45 offered no gain; T reductions lose revenue. Keep root and T fixed and tune B cautiously.

note: Adopt the island's best validated design, securing its higher C6 recovery and lower cost before the final cautious reflux probe.
notebook:
PLAN: Secure R1032's improved 1.274 baseline, then use the last two solves to probe the C6 reflux boundary cautiously (4.7, then 4.6 if purity remains comfortable). Root and C5 finisher stay fixed.
B35/4.8 improved BT recovery to 708 mol/s and revenue by $15M/yr while cutting cost. B30/4.5 collapsed purity to 94%, but the failure confounded stage and reflux changes. R1031 shows root changes are dangerous; R1034 shows T boil-up reduction fails convergence.

note: Make one isolated, small C6-column reflux reduction at fixed stages and cut point, targeting modest savings and higher recovery without approaching the known purity cliff too aggressively.
notebook:
PLAN: Secure R1032's improved 1.274 baseline, then use the last two solves to probe the C6 reflux boundary cautiously (4.7, then 4.6 if purity remains comfortable). Root and C5 finisher stay fixed. Now testing B reflux 4.7 only.
B35/4.8 improved BT recovery to 708 mol/s and revenue by $15M/yr while cutting cost. B30/4.5 collapsed purity to 94%, but that failure confounded stage and reflux changes. R1031 shows root changes are dangerous; R1034 shows T boil-up reduction fails convergence. R1063 confirms lower T reflux loses more C5 revenue than it saves.

note: Use the last solve at the midpoint of the known C6 purity cliff: 4.7 is profitable and 4.6 fails, so 4.65 may capture further recovery and savings while retaining the blend.
notebook:
PLAN: Preserve the validated 1.294 design and spend the final solve on the midpoint C6 reflux probe (4.65), since 4.7 is profitable while 4.6 misses blend purity. Root and C5 finisher remain fixed; the best valid design is retained regardless.
B35/4.7 gives 1.294, increasing BT recovery and lowering cost versus 4.8. R1091 shows B35/4.6 loses BT sale entirely, so the purity cliff lies between 4.6 and 4.7. Earlier aggressive stage/reflux cuts and T-column changes were unsuccessful.
